stem: the Isha Upanishad's first verse says "tena tyaktena bhunjitha." in its common reading, which takes bhunjitha as "enjoy," what does that phrase tell the reader to do?
options: renounce the world in order to reach heaven
enjoy the world while gathering more wealth
enjoy the world through renunciation
give up all action and live in the forest
why: In the common reading, Isha Upanishad 1 says "by that renounced, enjoy," then "do not covet: whose is wealth?" Because all this belongs to the Lord, letting go is the way to enjoy. (Shankara instead reads bhunjitha as "protect": guard the self through renunciation.)

es.stem: el primer verso de la Isha Upanishad dice "tena tyaktena bhunjitha". en su lectura común, que entiende bhunjitha como "disfruta", ¿qué le pide esa frase al lector?
options: renunciar al mundo para llegar al cielo
disfrutar del mundo mientras junta más riqueza
disfrutar del mundo a través de la renuncia
dejar toda acción e irse a vivir al bosque
es.why: En la lectura común, Isha Upanishad 1 dice "con eso renunciado, disfruta", y luego "no codicies: ¿de quién es la riqueza?". Como todo esto pertenece al Señor, soltar es la manera de disfrutar. (Shankara, en cambio, lee bhunjitha como "protege": cuida el ser mediante la renuncia.)

stem: in the Kena Upanishad's story, the gods boast of a victory, and Agni, the fire god, cannot burn a single blade of grass set before him by a mysterious being (a yaksha). what is the story teaching?
options: the gods' powers come from Brahman, not from the gods themselves
fire is the weakest of the gods, so it was tested first
the gods won their victory by the power of their own sacrifices
Brahman is seen by the eye once the gods have given up their pride
why: Kena Upanishad 3.1–4.1: the victory was Brahman's; without Brahman's power Agni cannot burn the grass and Vayu cannot move it, and Uma Haimavati tells Indra the being was Brahman.

es.stem: en el relato de la Kena Upanishad, los dioses presumen de una victoria, y Agni, el dios del fuego, no logra quemar una sola brizna de hierba que le pone delante un ser misterioso (un yaksha). ¿qué enseña el relato?
options: los poderes de los dioses vienen de Brahman, no de los dioses mismos
el fuego es el más débil de los dioses, por eso lo probaron primero
los dioses ganaron la victoria por la fuerza de sus propios sacrificios
Brahman se ve con los ojos cuando los dioses dejan de lado su orgullo
es.why: Kena Upanishad 3.1–4.1: la victoria era de Brahman; sin el poder de Brahman, Agni no puede quemar la hierba ni Vayu moverla, y Uma Haimavati le dice a Indra que aquel ser era Brahman.

stem: a merchant turns down a profitable but dishonest deal so as to keep his word. in the terms of the Katha Upanishad's two paths (1.2.1–2), what has he chosen?
options: preyas, the pleasant, over shreyas, the good
shreyas, the good, over preyas, the pleasant
artha, prosperity, over dharma, right conduct
kama, desire, over moksha, liberation
why: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1–2: the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person; the wise choose the good over the pleasant, as Nachiketa did when he refused Death's riches.

es.stem: un comerciante rechaza un negocio rentable pero deshonesto para cumplir su palabra. en los términos de los dos caminos de la Katha Upanishad (1.2.1–2), ¿qué eligió?
options: preyas, lo agradable, por encima de shreyas, lo bueno
shreyas, lo bueno, por encima de preyas, lo agradable
artha, la prosperidad, por encima de dharma, la recta conducta
kama, el deseo, por encima de moksha, la liberación
es.why: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1–2: lo bueno (shreyas) y lo agradable (preyas) se le presentan a cada persona; el sabio elige lo bueno por encima de lo agradable, como hizo Nachiketa al rechazar las riquezas de la Muerte.

stem: in the Mandukya Upanishad, the third quarter of the self, called prajna ("the knowing one"), is one mass of knowing, made of bliss. which state is its field?
options: the state of waking
the state of dreaming
the fourth, turiya
dreamless deep sleep
why: Mandukya Upanishad 5: where the sleeper desires nothing and sees no dream is deep sleep (sushupta); its knower, prajna, is a single mass of knowing, made of bliss.

es.stem: en la Mandukya Upanishad, el tercer cuarto del ser, llamado prajna ("el que conoce"), es una sola masa de conocer, hecha de dicha. ¿cuál es su campo?
options: el estado de estar despierto
el estado de sueño con sueños
el cuarto estado, turiya
el sueño profundo sin sueños
es.why: Mandukya Upanishad 5: donde el que duerme no desea nada ni ve ningún sueño, eso es el sueño profundo (sushupta); quien lo conoce, prajna, es una sola masa de conocer, hecha de dicha.

stem: according to Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita ("qualified non-dualism"), how are the world and individual souls related to God?
options: they are an illusion laid over Brahman, like a snake seen on a rope
they are fully real and exist entirely independent of God
they are a dream of God that ends when God wakes from it
they are real and form God's body, wholly dependent on God
why: Ramanuja (Sri Bhashya; Vedartha Sangraha) reads the inner-controller passage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (3.7) to mean that souls and matter are real and are the body of God, who is their inner self.

es.stem: según el Vishishtadvaita de Ramanuja ("no dualismo calificado"), ¿cómo se relacionan el mundo y las almas individuales con Dios?
options: son una ilusión sobre Brahman, como la serpiente en la cuerda
son plenamente reales y existen del todo independientes de Dios
son solo un sueño de Dios, que se acaba cuando él despierta
son reales y forman el cuerpo de Dios, dependientes de él
es.why: Ramanuja (Sri Bhashya; Vedartha Sangraha) lee el pasaje del controlador interno de la Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (3.7) como que las almas y la materia son reales y son el cuerpo de Dios, que es su ser interior.

stem: among the Bhagavad Gita's three kinds of gift (17.20–22), which kind is a gift given expecting something in return, or given grudgingly?
options: sattvic, of clarity and goodness
rajasic, of restless passion
tamasic, of dullness and inertia
daivi, of the divine qualities
why: Bhagavad Gita 17.21: a gift given for a return, for a reward, or reluctantly is rajasic; 17.20 calls a gift given simply because giving is right, expecting nothing back, sattvic.

es.stem: entre los tres tipos de regalo del Bhagavad Gita (17.20–22), ¿de qué tipo es un regalo dado esperando algo a cambio, o dado de mala gana?
options: sáttvico, de claridad y bondad
rajásico, de pasión inquieta
tamásico, de torpeza e inercia
daivi, de las cualidades divinas
es.why: Bhagavad Gita 17.21: un regalo dado por algo a cambio, por una recompensa o a regañadientes es rajásico; 17.20 llama sáttvico al regalo dado solo porque dar es lo correcto, sin esperar nada.

stem: according to the Mandukya Upanishad (verse 7), as Gaudapada and Shankara read it, what is "the fourth" (turiya), and why is it described mostly by what it is not?
why: Mandukya Upanishad 7 calls the fourth unseen, ungraspable, unthinkable and unnameable, yet peaceful, auspicious and not-two: "that is the self." Gaudapada's Karika treats it as the unchanging ground of waking, dream and deep sleep.

rubric.point: says the fourth is the self, pure awareness, that underlies or is present through waking, dreaming and deep sleep. calling it a further state that comes after deep sleep does not count.
says it is described by negation because it is not an object: it cannot be seen, grasped, thought or named the way things in the three states can. "because it is mysterious" alone does not count.
mentions any of the verse's positive marks (peaceful/shanta, auspicious/shiva, not-two/advaita) or links the fourth to the silence after a-u-m.

es.stem: según la Mandukya Upanishad (verso 7), tal como la leen Gaudapada y Shankara, ¿qué es "el cuarto" (turiya), y por qué se describe sobre todo por lo que no es?
es.why: Mandukya Upanishad 7 llama al cuarto invisible, inasible, impensable e innombrable, y a la vez pacífico, auspicioso y no-dos: "eso es el ser". La Karika de Gaudapada lo trata como el fondo inmutable de la vigilia, el sueño con sueños y el sueño profundo.

stem: in the Advaita Vedanta method of knowing the self, as taught by Shankara and his followers, what are shravana, manana and nididhyasana?
why: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 says the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on; Shankara and later Advaita teachers made these verbs a three-step method. Later schools weigh the steps differently: the Vivarana makes hearing the main means, the Bhamati gives meditation a larger role.
source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5; Shankara, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad Bhashya

rubric.point: shravana: hearing or studying the teaching of the Upanishads, usually from a teacher. "listening" with no mention of the teaching or scripture is partly met.
manana: reflecting or reasoning on what was heard until doubts about it are removed.

nididhyasana: sustained, deep contemplation of the teaching. either major Advaita account counts: dwelling on the teaching to remove contrary habits so that the knowledge born of hearing stands firm (Vivarana school, which makes shravana the main means), or meditation through which the purified mind gives rise to direct knowledge (Bhamati school). a general "meditation" with no link to the teaching is partly met.
names the source: Yajnavalkya's words to Maitreyi in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (2.4.5).

es.stem: en el método del Advaita Vedanta para conocer el ser, tal como lo enseñan Shankara y sus seguidores, ¿qué son shravana, manana y nididhyasana?
es.why: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 dice que el ser ha de ser visto, escuchado, reflexionado y meditado; Shankara y los maestros advaita posteriores hicieron de esos verbos un método de tres pasos. Las escuelas posteriores pesan los pasos de distinto modo: la Vivarana hace de la escucha el medio principal, la Bhamati da más lugar a la meditación.
